catalog_quote: Stress is limited to the last three syllables of the word. Final stress is uncommon in polysyllables and generally restricted to idiosyncratically stressed suffixes. The choice between penult and antepenult stress is in part rule-governed, in part a lexical property. The main generalizations are formulated and illustrated below: (13)a. V-final forms (i) antepenult stress: fór.fo.ta 'agitation', ... ré.pe.de 'fast' ... (ii) penult stress: če.tá.te 'fortress', ... re.pé.de 'rebukes' ... (iii) obligatory penult stress if penult is closed: al.bás.tru 'blue', a.prín.de 'lights up' ... b. C-final forms (i) penult stress: bí.vol 'buffalo' ... (ii) final stress: ... re.zul.tát 'result' ... (iii) obligatory final stress if final in -CC(C)#: as.fált 'asphalt', ... a.da.póst 'shelter'. ... sweep_summary: Five title hits for Romanian. Two are about word stress: Roca 1999 (Eurotyp chapter; paywalled at De Gruyter, WAF-blocked; the catalog already carries its StressTyp2 excerpt 1717) and Iscrulescu 2006 (Benjamins, closed; abstract obtained via OpenAlex and saved). The Iscrulescu abstract explicitly argues that Romanian nominal stress is weight-insensitive (syllabic trochees, final-consonant final stress as opacity), contra Steriade 1984's weight-sensitive analysis, so it contradicts the mechanism behind the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding at the analysis level; the full paper is high priority. Ulivi 1985 (secondary stress in Daco-Romanian dialects, RRL) is print-only (lingv.ro archive starts 2006) and concerns secondary stress. Göbbel 2003 and Swerts 2007 are sentence-level prosody (focus/pitch accent), not word stress; Swerts's TLDR ('accent distribution... demarcative rather than contrastive' in Romanian) was recorded. Iscrulescu's ROA 887 dissertation was fetched sources and checked: no stress-placement statement. No new first-hand statement supersedes Steriade 1984. DuckDuckGo/Bing/Google/HathiTrust/Internet Archive were unreachable or blocked from our machine, so discovery relied on Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, ROA and publisher/journal sites.

audit.recode_to: quantity-insensitive morphological/lexical: primary stress on the rightmost syllable of the stem (root + derivational suffixes/theme vowel), inflectional desinences outside the stress domain, plus a lexically marked stem-penult class (Chitoran 1996/2002); at minimum add a caution that the leading specialist analysis denies weight-sensitivity and re-read with Chitoran 2002 ch. on stress before keeping QS-HEDGED.

sources.quote: Summarises Chitoran 1996: two coexisting lexical patterns; 'In pattern 1, when the final syllable is CV, stress falls on the penultimate syllable... When the final syllable is CVC, the penultimate syllable is stressed'; 'Inflectional markers added at the right edge of the root ... are never stressed ... sources.citation: Chitoran, Ioana. 2002. The phonology and morphology of Romanian diphthongization. Probus 14(2): 205-246. doi:10.1515/prbs.2002.009 (author deposit hal-01226133)
sources.quote: p.208: 'Stress in Romanian falls on the rightmost syllable of the prosodic word. The prosodic word includes the root and derivational material, excluding inflections and desinence vowels. Thus, the penult is stressed when the final syllable contains the desinence vowel (4a), and the final syllable is stressed in the absence of a desinence vowel (4b).' p.209: 'Romanian also contains a lexically marked stress pattern, with penultimate stress' (kámer-ă, bívol). p.228: 'There is evidence, however, that the stress system of Romanian is not weight sensitive (Chitoran 1996, 1997, 2001).'

sources.quote: I show that nominal stress is best analyzed as weight-insensitive footing (syllabic trochees), contra claims that the system is weight-sensitive (moraic trochees, Steriade 1984). Forms with superficial final vowels are shown to conform to the syllabic trochee pattern (modulo certain items with lexical specification). The necessity of final vowel extrametricality, claimed in previous analyses of Romance stress, is obviated. Stress on the final syllable in words ending in consonants is claimed to represent an instance of phonological opacity
